Antonio

messages.subject: correction to example from tutorial
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

First, thanks for working on this package!  It looks very promising.

I am working through the examples in the tutorial using rmr version 1.2.  The tapply example returns in the tutorial is as follows:

  groups = rbinom(32, n = 50, prob = 0.4)
  groups = to.dfs(groups)
  from.dfs(mapreduce(input = groups,
                     map = function(k,v) keyval(v, NULL),
                     reduce = function(k,vv) keyval(k, length(vv)))

This returned a set of all zero counts.  The fix was to replace the map with this:

map = function(k,v) keyval(v, 1)

The NULL generated empty lists which then combined to create the empty list (hence the zero lengths).  Changing the return value to have length 1 fixed this.

I am new and only trying things now with version 1.2, so perhaps this is due to the version bump?

Thanks,
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a problem where my input data comes as a set of text csv files and I am hoping that RHadoop can help with processing the files.  I would like to map over the set of files, processing each file in its entirety by a single node.  All of the examples that I have seen show a single csv file being broken up and processed line-by-line.  For example,  suppose I have a list of csv files, each with columns x and y and I want to fit the linear model y ~ x for each file.  Can I do this with RHadoop?

Here's an example.  First, generate some data:

test1 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(10),
                    y = rnorm(10))
test2 <- data.frame(x = rnorm(10),
                    y = rnorm(10))
write.csv(test1, "test1.csv")
write.csv(test2, "test2.csv")

Just to illustrate what I want to do, here's the example with lapply:

files <- c("test1.csv", "test2.csv")
lapply(files, function(file) {
  dat <- read.csv(file)
  fm <- lm(y ~ x, dat)
  coef(fm)
})

But I am stuck when trying to convert this simple lapply into a parallel hadoop job.  Here's my best attempt (with pseudocode inserted where I need some help).

hdfs.put("test1.csv", "/temp/test1.csv")
hdfs.put("test2.csv", "/temp/test2.csv")

res <- mapreduce(input = c("/temp/test1.csv", "/temp/test1.csv"),
                 output = NULL,
                 map = function(k, v) {
                   dat <- read.csv(v)  ## This line does NOT work but is here for illustration
                   fm <- lm(y ~ x, dat)
                   keyval(k, coef(fm))
                 })

This does not work because it maps over each line in each of the files rather than sending each file to a node.

I know that I can work around this by using to.dfs() with the appropriate list of data.frame keyvals, but I am planning on using this on data that is too large to have all files read into R at once.

Thanks for any suggestions!
Ian

This default has been questioned by other users and I have dropped it in the experimental branch I was telling you about. The  new rule would be, pending community feedback, if a format doesn't have a specific way of denoting what the key is, like the sequence file format, then the key is going to be NULL and all the data is going to be in the second argument, the value. The reason why I picked the first column is that it is the hadoop streaming  default, but time and again I said that hadoop streaming is only the implementation layer and it is not a priority to stay close to Hadoop whereas it is a priority to adopt R language idioms and conventions. So what people said is that when they are reading a csv they expect a behavior like read.table, only that data is a read a bunch of rows at a time, with all the columns staying together. That's the behavior in branch multirec-io.

Going record at a time, scalability may be OK but efficiency is going to be pretty bad. It's just taxing the interpreter too much. We are in the process of looking into all the efficiency aspects but right now I would say

1) Download multirec-io tomorrow. It can read 1M rows in 22 seconds in a single process. I say tomorrow because there is one automated test that's failing, so I want to fix that first
2) If you can avoid sending all the points through the reduce phase, that would be best. The idea is: can you preprocess, filter, summarize right in the mapper? if yes, you should. In fast k means, I don't wait until the reducer to take averages, I start summing and counting points in the mapper and then finish it off in the reducer and only at the end I take the ratios. I don't know what the equivalent is for lm but I imagine that being linear it may be possible to do smaller lms separately and combine them. I don't know what the combination weights would be, I suppose something related to the RMS. This is intuition, so if the math is wrong please don't hold it against me. Roughly speaking the efficient pattern is: in the mapper, write your usual efficient R program, only that it works on a fraction of the input. In the reducer combine the outputs of the mapper. This usually doesn't work unless the program is trivial, so start making some changes. The changes are usually of the type: can we make the results of the mapper more "combinable"? For instance with averages one has just to delay taking the ratio because sum and counts of arbitrary subsets are associative and commutative, so this works. Sometimes it is as easy as augmenting the results of the mapper with a weight that we later use in the reducer to do a weighted sum. Linearity is your friend, but medians of medians work too, under certain conditions.
3) In your case the data is already grouped in each file and then we merge everything in one single mapreduce job and then split it in the reduce phase. This sounds wasteful (even if it is what I suggested). How about running a mapreduce job per file? How many of those do you have? Stil we are not guaranteed a single map even if the files are small. I don't have a good solution along this line of thinking, but I haven't given up yet.

You are welcome.
>
>
> Ian

There really isn't a way to make my reduce function associative or commutative.  The application I'm going for is to use Hadoop as a cluster management and job submission tool, where I want to run a bunch of jobs that are independent of one another over a cluster.  One mapreduce per file isn't too appealing because I'm looking at numbers of files in the order of 1k to 10k.

Yes I would say that is the end of that idea. The way R works, sending one record at a time through the shuffle phase is going to be slow, just because it takes the interpreter so much. In fact it taxes also the shuffle phase and it is not a recommended pattern even if you wrote Java, even if you can get away with it in that case. One thing you could do that is very general and can help is group your data with a tapply and then send it thought the reduce, not reduced in size or summarized but already grouped

map = function(k,v) tapply(v, sapply(v, compute.group), function(x) keyval(compute.group(x), x))

where compute.group is user-defined.
In the reduce you are going to get something nested, a list of this tapply computed groups so you will have to flatten it one level. If your number of groups is not huge, this means that there will be at most number of groups x number of mappers records in the shuffle phase, as opposed the initial number of records. The amount of data is the same, but R does more of the work in the C libs and mapreduce has fewer pieces to deal with in the shuffle phase. Actually, even the amount of data is less because of the serialization overhead (try a serialize(1, connection=NULL) to believe). So in summary, even if you can't do an in-map reduction, even if you can't do a combine or in addition to these it always pays off to move around few bigger records than many small ones.
I think rmr is no different from R in that naive programs are often slow, advanced ones can be 100X faster. rmr needs a combination of R optimization techniques and Hadoop optimization techniques.

Each reduce call is run on a single machine with all the data for that reduce in memory, but each reduce may process a tiny fraction of the data, this is program dependent. "reduce job" is a litlle confusing of a wording. Jobs have multiple, even millions of reduce calls. It is bad because for R-specific and Hadoop-specific reasons. R is vector oriented, so vector primitives are fast but the interpreter is slow, 120X C in certain cases. For Hadoop, the map phase is performed locally where the data is, with no network transmission penalties and reading disk sequentially. So the code is farmed out to the data, and not the other way around. This is a big shift from how we did things in the past. The shuffle phase, in between map and reduce, is a global communication phase that is inherently costly. So the more you get done in the map, the better. Cascading even uses techniques where multiple jobs are run instead of one just to make the reduce phase lighter (filtered joins) and it pays off in a range of applications.
